excerpt: Replay past conversations with your AI assistants. See every message and tool call in a chat-like view.
**LLM Calls** shows individual model requests. Use it to compare models, prompts, token usage, cost, and response performance without reviewing an entire conversation or trace.
**Traces** shows end-to-end agent runs and the application work around them.
View agent executions, model costs, token usage, tool calls, and recent errors in the Agents Dashboards.
You can also instrument agents manually by following our [manual instrumentation guides](/platforms/python/agent-tracing/manual-instrumentation/).
Sentry uses the `gen_ai.conversation.id` attribute to group related AI spans, and some SDK integrations set it automatically.
The Model Cost widget shows estimated costs based on token usage and model pricing.
The Tools dashboard displays Tool Calls and Tool Errors widgets, as well as all used tools with durations and errors:
Click on any trace to open the [AI Spans view](#ai-spans-view) in Explore → Traces.
**Handoffs**: Agent-to-agent transitions and human handoffs
Supported AI libraries are instrumented automatically when their packages are installed.
Your agent will set up Sentry in your Python app automatically. Works with Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, and more.
Use `set_conversation_id()` so every AI span in a chat session shares the same `gen_ai.conversation.id`.
To keep other PII on but turn AI content off, set `include_prompts=False` on the integration.
Any of `id`, `email`, or `username` is sufficient — the Conversations tab displays whichever fields are present.
Sentry is the debugging platform that helps every developer detect, trace, and fix issues.
Drop in the [SDK](https://sentry.io/platforms/). No agents to install. No performance surprises.
Find root causes and fix production issues with [Seer, our debugging agent](https://sentry.io/product/seer/).
[Agent tracing](https://sentry.io/product/tracing/ai-agent/) helps you catch unexpected output issues, bad tool calls and visualize the spend and performance across all your agents.
Debug 500's, trace slow requests, replay fetch() failures, and fix the broken code that caused it.
Catch slow queries, N+1s, and request timeouts before the ‘why is this so slow?’ posts fill up your feed.
Map every incident to the release, PR, and owner -- automatically.
Fixes what’s broken while you ship what’s next – generating precise, merge-ready patches.
You can also replay past conversations.
Use it to replay a user's multi-turn interaction, inspect its transcript and timeline, and find where a response or tool call went wrong.
Use it to compare models, prompts, token usage, cost, and response performance without reviewing an entire conversation or trace.
Use it to follow execution across model calls, tools, and services or to investigate latency and errors in context.
Below these widgets is a traces table showing trace ID, agents, root duration, errors, LLM calls, tool calls, total tokens, total cost, and timestamp.
**Duration**: Displays average and P95 response times for your agent executions
Prompt and response content is off by default — use the `gen_ai` key of the [`data_collection` option](/platforms/python/configuration/options/#data_collection) to capture it.
The [Conversations](/product/agents/conversations/) view includes a **User** column.
As of SDK version `11.0.0`, Sentry auto-instruments the most popular AI SDKs and frameworks out of the box — you don't need to add their integrations yourself.
You can also set `recordInputs` / `recordOutputs` on a specific AI integration.
Agent Tracing data is fully connected to your other Sentry data like logs, errors, and traces.

Long-time Sentry users say the fully open-source code helped them build advanced integrations because they could read exactly what the code does instead of relying on docs. They plan to stay customers despite the BSL relicense.

One user calls the move to the Business Source License very disappointing. They had planned to use Sentry for a side project but will now look for an alternative or use an old version, because they refuse to rely on closed-source software.

A user has run self-hosted Sentry at work for a couple of years and says it has worked fantastically and is rock-solid once running. They also use the SaaS version for freelance work. Self-hosted releases lag behind the SaaS launches, which they find understandable.
A Sentry cloud user says they are happy with the product and are reassured that they could host their own instance if the cloud costs became too high.

A user says they love Sentry for its very responsive support, open-source code, nice UI, no nagging, and a fair price. They say hosting with Sentry is cheaper than self-hosting, even though self-hosting is well documented.

Complaint: Sentry samples exceptions, so the user can't rely on it to see every single instance. Because they need every exception logged, Sentry 'feels quite useless' to them and they wouldn't choose it for their next project, though otherwise it has been fantastic.
A user who has used hosted Sentry for a couple of years says it works really well for its price and recommends it highly.
A user built a mobile crash-reporting solution on top of self-hosted Sentry and calls it a great product.

A customer says Sentry has exceptional customer service, with prompt, useful responses or bug fixes every time. They rely on its native crash reporting for an open-source game engine and say it was very simple to integrate. Without it, resolving user crashes would be '1000x harder'.

One team self-hosts Sentry on a high-end Hetzner server (96 cores, 512GB) for about $300/month. They process around 25M transactions per day, which they estimate would cost tens of thousands on the managed version. Early on, they had to add Kafka partitions and processor replicas, otherwise backpressure filled Redis until it ran out of memory.
A user deployed self-hosted Sentry with a Helm chart and says it 'just works'. Over the years they had a few incidents that required wiping Kafka queues.
A user says the amount of shell script needed to install is a no-go for them. They also object to spinning up a 16GB machine at minimum just to track errors from 4–8GB production VPSes.

Sentry was straightforward to deploy years ago but is now 'self host-able but increasingly prohibitively complex'. This team found Kubernetes plus a Helm chart on bare metal the only practical approach. It runs well if you can throw hardware and engineering time at it.

A user who has self-hosted Sentry for 10+ years says installation is git clone, editing one or two config files, and running ./install.sh. The 16GB RAM is needed only for the full feature set, such as session replay and end-to-end tracing. They praise the self-hosting team as helpful on Discord.
A user who uses Sentry with most clients has to spin up their own Sentry in Docker for local debugging. They find it heavy on their machine, especially alongside Grafana and Prometheus.
A startup used Sentry for distributed tracing of high-volume IoT events. The bill reached $3–5k from tracing alone, so they tried to self-host and were 'flabbergasted' by the project's complexity.

One user left managed Sentry for GDPR reasons. They only needed unhandled-exception alerts, so they replaced it with a Django logging handler that stores tracebacks in a database table, plus a daily email digest.

A user who runs both hosted and self-hosted Sentry prefers hosted because there is less to manage. They say self-hosting is fine if budgeted and recommend it only for legal or compliance needs. It truly broke once, on the upgrade from version 9 to date-based versioning, and starting over was easier.

A team has self-hosted two Sentry instances for about 8 years with 20GB RAM each. About 90% of updates went smoothly; the rest had problems, all solved via the issue tracker. They are a bit afraid of updates but call it a fairly easy self-host and 'an amazing piece of software'.
A user still loves Sentry but says it is now so enormous that self-hosting isn't practical for smaller businesses.
